purpose: 363-item candidate research pool with at least three primary-role indicators for every headline and primary construct. Cognitive review is not an active project gate. Not psychometrically validated.
itemIdPolicy: Permanent IDs use <domain>I<3 digits>. IDs are never reused after retirement.

items.text: An action can be morally wrong even if every person who knows about it approves of it.
An action cannot be morally wrong independently of people's attitudes toward it.
A moral rule can have genuine exceptions even when everyone agrees on the relevant facts.
Some moral requirements can bind a person even when following them conflicts with that person's own goals and preferences.
Two fully informed people disagree about whether an action is morally wrong. Which description best fits the disagreement?

options.label: At least one of them must be mistaken about a moral fact.
Each claim can be correct relative to the individual making it.
Each claim can be correct relative to a social or cultural framework.
Both are treating morality as factual when such moral facts do not exist.
Their moral statements need not be literal claims that are true or false.
None of these descriptions fits well.

items.text: When one action would produce much better overall consequences than another, that difference can by itself be a strong moral reason to choose it.
Some actions remain wrong even when performing them would clearly produce the best overall outcome.
A good moral judgment should ask what kind of person an action expresses or helps someone become.
A stranger's well-being should count just as much as the same amount of well-being for someone close to me.

A rescue team can save five trapped people only by deliberately causing serious but nonfatal harm to one uninvolved person who would otherwise be safe. There is no alternative. Which response is closest to your view?

options.label: Deliberately injuring the person is impermissible regardless of the numbers.
It is normally impermissible, with only exceptional cases possibly overriding that.
The answer depends on further details not given here.
It is normally permissible when it is the only way to save substantially more people.
It is permissible, and may be required, if it clearly produces the best outcome.

items.text: Preventing needless suffering is an important consideration when deciding whether conduct is morally acceptable.
People should have equal moral standing even when they differ greatly in status, wealth, or social importance.
Fairness often requires rewards or burdens to reflect what people contributed.
Loyalty to a group can be a moral virtue even when remaining loyal involves personal sacrifice.
Respecting established roles and authorities can have moral value apart from the immediate consequences.
Some acts can be morally degrading or defiling even when they cause no obvious material harm.
Thinking independently and developing my own ideas.
Personal safety and a secure immediate environment.
Demonstrating competence and accomplishing difficult things.
Justice and protection for people beyond my own social circles.
Rank these values from most important to least important when they genuinely conflict.

options.label: Choosing and directing my own actions.
Protecting personal safety and stability.
Accomplishing difficult things and demonstrating competence.
Preserving inherited customs and ways of life.
Protecting the rights and welfare of people generally.

items.text: Even a belief I am highly confident in should remain open to revision if sufficiently strong contrary evidence appears.
Some beliefs can become so well justified that future contrary evidence should not normally reopen them.
Direct observation is an especially important source of evidence about how the world works.
Methods that expose claims to systematic testing deserve more confidence than methods that cannot be checked in comparable ways.
When I cannot evaluate a technical claim myself, agreement among qualified experts should count as substantial evidence.
Reality may include fundamental entities or powers that no natural science could, even in principle, fully describe.
Everything that exists is ultimately physical, even if some physical systems have very complex properties.
At least some abstract objects, such as numbers, exist independently of human thought and language.
Purposes or ends are genuine features of at least some natural processes, not merely descriptions imposed by observers.
Nature itself contains no purposes; talk of purpose is something observers add when describing natural processes.
A complete account of the brain and its physical processes could, in principle, fully explain consciousness.
What makes a future person the same person as me depends mainly on psychological continuity such as memory, intentions, and character.
The self is better understood as an ongoing process or organization than as a separate inner substance that remains unchanged.
A notebook, computer, or other external tool can sometimes become a genuine part of a person's cognitive process rather than merely an aid to it.
A machine scans you perfectly, destroys your body, and creates an exact functioning duplicate elsewhere with all your memories and dispositions. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: The duplicate is straightforwardly the same person.
Something important survives, but strict numerical identity is unclear or lost.
The duplicate is a new person despite the perfect continuity.
The answer depends on a further fact about persons or consciousness.
None of these descriptions fits well.

items.text: Human beings sometimes exercise genuine control over which action they choose.
Given the complete state of the world and the laws governing it, only one future is physically possible.
A person can sometimes deserve moral blame for an action even after every causal explanation of why they acted has been given.
Many important human dispositions can change substantially when environments, incentives, and institutions change.
A person's conscious reasons can make a causal difference to what they do.
Which option is closest to your current view about divine reality?

options.label: At least one personal or agent-like God probably exists.
Some divine or sacred reality probably exists, but not as a personal agent.
I am substantially uncertain whether any divine reality exists.
Probably no divine reality exists.
No divine reality exists.

items.text: If some divine reality exists, it is more likely to be capable of intentions than to be wholly impersonal.
At least some part of reality is genuinely supernatural rather than entirely natural.
Some important aspect of a person can continue to exist after biological death.
Human life is part of an objective purpose built into reality rather than a purpose created only by human beings.
A human life can have objective meaning even if the person living it does not experience that life as meaningful.
People can create genuine meaning through their projects, relationships, and commitments even if the universe supplies no purpose for them.
Human life has no objective meaning independent of what people create or value.
The world generally contains many worthwhile possibilities that can be discovered or created.
Individuals have moral claims that should not be overridden merely because doing so would benefit a larger group.
Some groups can have legitimate goals that cannot be reduced entirely to the separate goals of their individual members.
Who a person is depends in important ways on relationships and social roles, not only on traits inside that individual.
A stranger on the other side of the world can have moral claims on me as weighty as those of someone in my own community.
When the two genuinely conflict, which consideration should normally receive greater moral priority?

options.label: A: Special obligations arising from membership in one's close group.
B: Equal consideration of people regardless of group membership.

items.text: A political institution can sometimes have a genuine moral right to impose rules by force, not merely the practical ability to do so.
People normally have a moral duty to obey valid laws because they are laws, even when they independently disagree with the rule.
Important political decisions should generally be made by a central authority capable of applying one rule across the whole jurisdiction.
Political power should generally be dispersed among smaller or overlapping institutions even when that produces more variation between places.
Rank these coordination mechanisms by how much weight they should generally carry when more than one is feasible.

options.label: Decentralized voluntary exchange and prices.
Collective or democratic decision-making by affected participants.
Expert or administrative planning based on specialized knowledge.

items.text: Once the relevant facts are known, the same moral rule should yield the same judgment across cases.
A moral requirement gives a person a reason to act only when it connects to something that person already wants or values.
Some moral questions cannot be settled by applying general rules alone; the particular features of the case can be decisive.
Moral judgment should take seriously the needs created by dependence, vulnerability, and ongoing relationships.
What kind of character an action expresses should matter less than whether the action itself was right or wrong.
It can be reasonable to give greater moral weight to the serious interests of people close to me than to equal interests of distant strangers.
Whether someone suffers does not by itself tell us whether an action is morally wrong.
Loyalty to a group has no moral value apart from whether the group is actually doing something good.
If no one is harmed or wronged, disgust or impurity alone is not a moral reason to condemn an act.
Novelty, excitement, and change.
Pleasure and enjoyment.
Caring for the well-being of people close to me.
Reasoning alone can sometimes justify knowledge without relying on new observation.
A claim can deserve high confidence even when it cannot be tested by systematic empirical methods.
Longstanding traditions can preserve knowledge that no single generation could easily reconstruct for itself.
Higher-level properties can always, in principle, be fully explained by the behavior and arrangement of their lower-level parts.
Some higher-level properties are genuinely novel and cannot be fully reduced to descriptions of their lower-level parts.
At least some features of mind or reality are fundamentally nonphysical.
Even a complete physical description of the brain could leave something about conscious experience unexplained.
There is a persisting subject of experience that remains the same self through major changes in memory and personality.
Continuity of the living body matters more to personal identity than continuity of memories or personality.
Without coercion or reward, people are often naturally capable of sustained cooperation and concern for others.
Even under favorable institutions, self-interest and competition remain powerful default tendencies in human behavior.
Many basic human dispositions remain fairly stable even when social conditions change substantially.
Reality is entirely natural; there are no genuinely supernatural beings, forces, or realms.
When biological death permanently ends brain function, the person no longer exists in any form.
Any purpose human life has is created by people rather than built into reality itself.
If the universe supplies no objective purpose, human projects cannot create genuine meaning by themselves.
A human life can have objective meaning without being part of a cosmic or divine purpose.
For ordinary people, the world is generally more dangerous than safe.
A society can remain healthy even when its members hold sharply different values and ways of life.
Humans are one part of ecological systems and should not treat the rest of nature merely as a resource for human purposes.
Social categories usually reflect stable underlying differences rather than mainly historical conventions.
A political system has a stronger claim to legitimacy when those subject to its rules have a meaningful and roughly equal role in authorizing it.
Political freedom primarily means having a protected sphere in which others do not interfere with one's choices.
Some individual rights should constrain what governments may do even when violating those rights would benefit a large majority.
A genuine moral requirement should apply to any person in the same morally relevant circumstances, regardless of who they are.
A moral principle is defective if some person affected by it could reasonably reject it as a basis for governing everyone.
Mutually advantageous agreement among people with different interests can provide a foundation for moral rules.
People may permissibly give substantial priority to their own projects even when they could produce somewhat more good by setting those projects aside.
Moral obligations can sometimes require very large personal sacrifices when much greater harm to others can thereby be prevented.
Directly causing a harm is normally morally worse than merely allowing an equally serious harm to occur.
Having influence or authority over other people.
Having substantial control over money, property, or other valuable resources.
Protecting my public image and avoiding humiliation.
Stability and safety for society as a whole.
Following rules and formal obligations even when doing so is inconvenient.
Avoiding actions that upset or embarrass people around me.
Remaining modest about my own importance and accomplishments.
Being someone the people close to me can reliably depend on.
Protecting the natural environment for its own sake.
Understanding and accepting people whose beliefs or ways of life differ sharply from mine.
Knowledge in complex fields is usually made of interconnected claims that can change as new evidence and concepts develop.
For at least some questions, human inquiry can arrive at answers that are objectively correct rather than merely useful or conventional.
A strong intuitive seeming can sometimes provide genuine justification for a belief even before supporting evidence is available.
A revelation believed to come from a divine or supernatural source can sometimes provide genuine knowledge.
When a mature scientific theory repeatedly succeeds, that is evidence that at least some of the unobservable entities or structures it describes are approximately real.
Important human behavior usually results from several interacting causes rather than one dominant kind of cause.
Biological differences and inherited dispositions can make a substantial causal contribution to human behavior.
Motives or processes outside conscious awareness can make a substantial causal difference to what people do.
A divine or supernatural agent can sometimes influence ordinary events in the world.
Events can sometimes occur through genuinely miraculous action rather than through ordinary natural processes alone.
A message believed to be genuine divine revelation can legitimately guide what a person ought to believe or do.
Some things can possess a sacred status that gives us reasons not to treat them merely as ordinary objects or resources.
Religious or spiritual commitments in my life.
Some social groups should have greater power and status than other groups.
Reducing large differences in social standing between groups is not, by itself, an important social goal.
People can often solve shared problems best through voluntary cooperation rather than by trying to defeat one another.
Competition between people or groups is often a healthy way to discover who can perform better or use resources more effectively.
Many social categories exist partly because people collectively create, maintain, and interpret them through social practices.
Political coercion requires meaningful consent from the people subjected to it in order to be fully legitimate.
A person is politically unfree when another person or institution holds uncontrolled power over them, even if that power is rarely exercised.
Freedom sometimes requires more than noninterference; people may also need real capabilities and opportunities to pursue important choices.
Rank these distributive principles by how much weight they should usually receive when allocating important social resources.

options.label: Equality: distribute shares as equally as possible.
Need: give more to those with greater needs.
Desert: give more to those who contributed or earned more.
Sufficiency: ensure everyone reaches an adequate threshold first.
Priority: give extra weight to improving the position of those who are worse off.
Entitlement: preserve holdings that arose through legitimate acquisition and transfer.

items.text: When people acquire and transfer property without force or fraud, they gain strong moral claims against others taking or controlling it.
Some productive resources can legitimately be owned in common rather than by particular individuals or firms.
A decision can be just because it was reached through fair procedures even when the resulting outcome is unequal or disappointing.
A procedure can be fair in form yet still produce an unjust result that institutions have reason to correct.
Wrongdoers can deserve punishment because of what they did, even when punishing them would have no beneficial future effects.
A central purpose of punishment is to discourage future wrongdoing by making harmful conduct costly.
A central purpose of justice after wrongdoing should be to repair harm, rehabilitate offenders, and restore workable relationships where possible.
Political institutions should take the interests of people outside their own country seriously even when doing so brings no reciprocal national benefit.
Shared national membership can create special political obligations to compatriots that do not extend equally to everyone in the world.
Overlapping and competing institutions can sometimes govern better than assigning final authority to one unified institution.
Religious doctrines or authorities should have independent standing as a source of public law, not merely influence citizens as private beliefs.
A moral requirement can legitimately apply to one person but not another even when their morally relevant circumstances are the same.
When a well-established moral principle and the particular features of a case point in different directions, which should normally receive greater weight?

options.label: A: The general principle.
B: The particular features of the case.

items.text: An action can be morally acceptable even when another available action would predictably produce much better consequences for everyone affected.
A strong moral prohibition can be overridden when violating it is the only way to prevent a vastly greater harm.
What people owe one another depends partly on relationships of care and dependence that impersonal rules can miss.
A principle is harder to justify morally when some person burdened by it has a reasonable basis for rejecting it as a rule for everyone.
A proposed moral rule has less force when everyone affected could instead agree to another rule that leaves each of them better off.

A surgeon can save three patients only by deliberately using an unwilling healthy person in a way that will seriously harm that person. Doing so would be permissible if the total benefit were large enough.
Parents normally have stronger moral obligations to protect their own children than to protect unfamiliar children facing the same level of need.
A person's own projects do not by themselves justify producing less good for others when the sacrifice required is manageable.
Morality should not normally require sacrifices so severe that a person can no longer pursue a decent life of their own.
There is an important moral difference between directly causing a serious harm and failing to prevent an equally serious harm.
When two people have the same morally relevant claim, giving one lower standing because of social rank is unfair.
People who contribute more to a shared project can fairly receive more of its benefits.
Defying a legitimate authority can be morally wrong even when the immediate consequences of defiance are harmless.
Questioning accepted ideas and reaching my own conclusions.
Being free to choose how I live and act.
Seeking new experiences that break routine.
Enjoying life's pleasures.
Being in a position where I can direct what other people do.
Having enough wealth or resources to control major opportunities.
Avoiding loss of face or public shame.
Living in a society protected from disorder and major threats.
Keeping customs handed down by my family, culture, or religion.
Obeying legitimate rules even when I would rather not.
Avoiding behavior likely to offend or seriously inconvenience people around me.
Not putting myself above other people.
Helping people I care about when they need me.
Being reliable to the people who depend on me.
Protecting ecosystems and nonhuman life.
Being willing to live alongside people with unfamiliar beliefs or ways of life.
Most important questions have fairly simple answers once the relevant facts are known.
Some important questions may remain permanently beyond the limits of human knowledge.
When careful observation conflicts with an attractive theory, the observation should normally carry more weight.
Without empirical evidence, reasoning alone cannot establish substantive facts about reality.
Expert consensus should count for little unless I can personally verify the reasoning or evidence behind it.
The fact that a belief has survived for many generations gives it some additional credibility.
An intuition unsupported by further reasons or evidence should not count as genuine justification for a belief.
A sincere experience interpreted as revelation should not by itself justify factual claims about the world.
A scientific theory can be highly successful even if the unobservable entities it describes do not literally exist.
Everything that exists belongs to the natural world, even if science has not yet explained all of it.
Talk of numbers, properties, or universals need not commit us to abstract objects that exist independently of concrete things and language.
Even when an external device is indispensable to someone's reasoning, the device remains a tool outside that person's mind.
A person's choices can genuinely be their own even when those choices have prior causes.
Exactly the same total conditions and laws could still allow more than one physically possible future.
If an action is fully explained by causes for which the person was never responsible, basic desert-based blame no longer makes sense.
People often help others simply because they care, even when no reward or punishment is involved.
Self-interest and competition are not unavoidable default tendencies in human behavior.
Most important human behavior can be explained adequately by one or two dominant kinds of cause.
Biology contributes little to stable differences in human behavior compared with learning and social environment.
Social institutions and learned environments can strongly shape behavior even when biological differences are small.
Conscious deliberation usually reflects causes already at work rather than making an independent causal difference to what a person does.
A motive should not count as a real cause of behavior unless the person is consciously aware of it.
At least one divine or godlike reality probably exists.
Any divine reality that exists is more likely to be impersonal than to have intentions or preferences.
Even if supernatural reality exists, it does not intervene in ordinary events.
All events occur through natural processes; genuinely miraculous events do not occur.
A claimed revelation should not carry authority merely because it is sincerely believed to have a divine source.
Nothing has a sacred status that places it beyond ordinary practical evaluation.
Taking part in religious or spiritual reflection and practice.
Which description is closest to your view of life's meaning?

options.label: At least some lives have meaning because of objective features independent of what anyone values.
Meaning is created by people through what they value, pursue, or care about.
Meaning can involve both objective features and what people value or create.
There is no genuine meaning to life in either sense.
None of these descriptions fits well.

items.text: The interests of a larger group can sometimes take priority over an individual's separate projects simply because the group's welfare is at stake.
Only individuals can literally have goals or obligations; talk of a group's goals is shorthand for the goals of its members.
A person's core identity could remain essentially the same even if most of their social relationships and roles changed.
A society has no general reason to accommodate ways of life that conflict sharply with the majority's values.
No social group should have higher status merely because it belongs to a supposedly superior category of people.
Reducing unjustified differences in social standing between groups is an important social goal.
When people pursue competing interests, competition usually coordinates them better than deliberate cooperation does.
Competition often damages outcomes that people could improve through cooperation.
Membership in a social category rarely reveals a deep and fixed essence shared by all its members.
Major social categories exist independently of the practices through which people classify and treat one another.
When serious human welfare and preservation of nonhuman nature conflict, human welfare should normally take priority.
No political institution has a moral right to coerce people merely by virtue of being their government.
The fact that a rule is legally valid does not by itself create any moral duty to obey it.
Political authority can be legitimate without each person's consent if it is justified in other ways.
A political order can be fully legitimate even when ordinary people have no meaningful role in authorizing its rulers or laws.
Interference with a person's choices is not necessarily a loss of freedom when the interference improves that person's range of worthwhile options.
A person can be fully free even when someone else holds arbitrary power over them, provided that power is not actually used.
A lack of resources or capabilities can be unfortunate without itself making a person less free, so long as no one interferes with them.
Individual rights may be overridden whenever doing so would produce sufficiently large benefits for everyone else.
A community has ten identical housing units and must assign them among people with different needs, contributions, and prior claims. Which consideration should receive the greatest weight?

options.label: Give everyone as equal a share or chance as possible.
Give priority to those whose need is greatest.
Give priority to those who contributed or earned more.
First ensure everyone reaches an adequate minimum.
Give extra weight to improving the position of those who are worst off.
Honor prior legitimate claims even if the final distribution is unequal.

items.text: Property claims can sometimes be overridden for important collective purposes even when the owner acquired the property without force or fraud.
Productive resources should normally have identifiable individual or organizational owners rather than be held in common.
Prices and voluntary exchange should usually play only a minor role in coordinating production when deliberate coordination is feasible.
When voluntary exchange can coordinate an activity adequately, collective decision-making should normally not direct the details of production or allocation.
Experts should advise public decisions, but specialized knowledge alone should not give administrators authority to choose for everyone else.
A fair procedure does not make an outcome more just when the result is substantively unjust.
When a procedure is genuinely fair, its outcome should normally stand even if the resulting distribution seems substantively undesirable.
Punishing a wrongdoer would be pointless if doing so produced no future benefit such as deterrence, protection, rehabilitation, or repair.
Deterring future wrongdoing is not, by itself, a sufficient reason to punish a person.
Justice after serious wrongdoing need not aim at rehabilitating the offender or restoring damaged relationships.
A government's primary political obligations are to its own members, even when outsiders could be helped at comparable cost.
Shared national membership by itself creates no stronger political obligation to compatriots than to equally situated people elsewhere.
For each area of law or governance, there should ultimately be one institution with final authority to settle conflicts among institutions.
Public law should never treat a religious doctrine as an independent reason for coercion merely because that doctrine is religiously authoritative.
Close relationships can create special moral obligations to particular people that do not exist toward strangers.
People with similar biological dispositions can develop very different patterns of behavior when their social environments differ substantially.
Everyone in a community approves of breaking a promise to an outsider because doing so benefits the community. Assume everyone knows all the relevant facts. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: The action can still be morally wrong even if everyone approves.
It is wrong only if some relevant person's or group's attitudes condemn it.
Its moral status depends on the standards or framework being used.
There is no stance-independent moral fact that settles the case.

items.text: Two rescue plans are identical except that one will save ten people and the other will save two. How much moral weight should that difference normally carry?

options.label: Usually decisive unless another very strong moral reason points the other way.
A strong reason, but readily outweighed by other moral considerations.
A modest reason among many.
Little or no moral weight by itself.

items.text: Someone can prevent a serious injury only by breaking a promise made to an innocent person. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: The promise should be kept; the constraint remains binding.
The promise strongly matters but may be overridden by sufficiently serious harm.
The promise is one consideration to weigh directly against the consequences.
Preventing the greater harm should determine the choice.

items.text: Two people perform the same helpful act. One acts from genuine generosity; the other acts only to improve their reputation. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: The difference in character or motive makes a major moral difference.
It makes some moral difference, though the act itself matters more.
It makes little moral difference if the outward act and consequences are the same.
It makes no moral difference.

items.text: Two people have the same urgent need, but one depends on you through an ongoing relationship of care. Does that relationship create an additional moral reason to help them?

options.label: Yes, a strong additional reason.
Yes, some additional reason.
No; equal need should be treated equally regardless of relationship.
Only if the relationship involved a specific prior commitment.

items.text: You can prevent the same amount of serious suffering either for one person you know well or for an unfamiliar person far away. Which consideration should matter more?

options.label: A: The fact that the person is close to me.
B: Neither; equal suffering should count equally.

items.text: A person can prevent five deaths only by deliberately imposing a severe injury on one unwilling bystander who would otherwise be unharmed. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: Impermissible regardless of the number saved.
Normally impermissible, but extreme cases may justify it.
Permissible when the expected benefit is sufficiently greater.
Required when it clearly produces the best overall outcome.

items.text: When judging whether an action is morally acceptable, how relevant is whether someone suffered physical or emotional harm?
When judging whether a social arrangement is morally acceptable, how relevant is whether some people are treated as having lower moral standing than others?
When judging whether an outcome is fair, how relevant is whether rewards and burdens reflect people's contributions?
When judging someone's conduct, how relevant is whether they betrayed people or groups to whom they owed loyalty?
When judging someone's conduct, how relevant is whether they violated a legitimate duty attached to their role or position?
When judging an act, how relevant is whether it is degrading, defiling, or contaminating even when direct harm is absent?
Having freedom to explore ideas that others around me reject.
Making major choices about my own life without others deciding for me.
Having adventure and variety in my life.
Having opportunities for enjoyable sensory experiences.
Reaching ambitious goals that demonstrate my ability.
Avoiding serious threats to my own health, home, and immediate safety.
Honoring customs that connect me to earlier generations.
Responding when someone close to me needs care or support.
Protecting the basic rights and welfare of people regardless of nationality or social group.
You are very confident in a belief, but a new source provides strong, well-supported evidence against it. Which is closest to how the belief should be treated?

options.label: Reopen the belief substantially and reassess it.
Lower confidence somewhat but keep the belief unless more evidence appears.
Keep the belief unless the new evidence becomes overwhelming.
Prior justification should make later contrary evidence largely irrelevant.

items.text: A carefully controlled observation conflicts with an elegant theory that has otherwise worked well. Which should normally receive more weight at first?

options.label: A: The observation.
B: The established theory.

items.text: Which is the clearest case of something that can be justified without new observation?

options.label: A conclusion following from logic or conceptual relations.
A claim about an unfamiliar physical object.
A claim about a past event.
No substantive claim can be justified without observation.

items.text: Two methods disagree. One produces public, repeatable tests; the other relies on private experiences that cannot be independently checked. Which deserves more confidence?

options.label: A: The publicly testable method.
B: The private-experience method.

items.text: Qualified specialists overwhelmingly agree about a technical question, but the conclusion conflicts with your own first impression. Which should normally receive more weight?

options.label: A: The expert consensus.
B: My own first impression.

items.text: Which description is closest to your view of reality as a whole?

options.label: Everything that exists is part of the natural world.
The natural world is central, but genuinely supernatural reality remains a live possibility.
Reality includes genuinely supernatural beings, powers, or realms.
None of these descriptions fits well.

items.text: Which description is closest to your view of minds and other apparently nonphysical phenomena?

options.label: They are ultimately entirely physical.
They depend on the physical but have higher-level properties not captured by simple reduction.
At least some are fundamentally nonphysical.
None of these descriptions fits well.

items.text: Suppose a complete account of every lower-level part of a system still fails to explain one stable higher-level property. Which interpretation is closest to your view?

options.label: The lower-level account is still incomplete; a full reduction should be possible in principle.
The higher-level property may be genuinely emergent and not fully reducible.
Both descriptions may be useful without settling the metaphysics.
None of these descriptions fits well.

items.text: Which statement is closest to your view of purpose in nature?

options.label: At least some natural processes have purposes built into reality.
Purpose exists only where agents or designers introduce it.
Purpose-language can be useful shorthand without describing a real purposive feature.
Purpose has no legitimate role in explaining natural processes.

items.text: Imagine neuroscience completely explains every function of the brain but some people still ask why conscious experience feels like anything from the inside. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: Nothing further would remain to be explained in principle.
A genuine explanatory question about experience could remain.
The remaining question would show that something nonphysical is involved.
None of these descriptions fits well.

items.text: A person gradually changes memories, values, personality, and relationships over many decades while remaining biologically continuous. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: A persisting self remains fundamentally the same subject through the changes.
The self is the continuing process formed by those changing psychological and biological relations.
Whether it is 'the same self' is mainly a practical or conventional question.
None of these descriptions fits well.

items.text: Assume a person's choice results from their own stable values and reasoning in a world where every event has prior causes. Could that choice still be genuinely free?

options.label: Yes, genuine freedom can be compatible with that causal history.
Possibly, depending on the kind of causal control the person has.
No, genuine freedom requires more than being caused by the person's values and reasoning.
None of these descriptions fits well.

items.text: Imagine the universe were reset to exactly the same total state, with exactly the same laws. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: Exactly the same future would have to occur.
More than one future could still occur.
The answer depends on whether the fundamental laws themselves are deterministic.
None of these descriptions fits well.

items.text: A person's harmful action results from manipulation that shaped their motives without their awareness. How much basic moral blame does the person deserve?

options.label: Roughly the same basic blame as without the manipulation.
Some blame, but substantially reduced.
No basic desert-based blame, though other responses may still be justified.
It depends on whether the person could recognize and resist the manipulation.

items.text: Someone anonymously returns a lost wallet containing a large amount of money when there is no realistic chance of reward or punishment. How informative is this about ordinary human capacity for benevolence?

options.label: Strong evidence that people can act from genuine concern for others.
Some evidence, though other motives may still be involved.
Little evidence about general human benevolence.
No meaningful evidence; self-interest can explain such behavior.

items.text: In a setting where cooperation is rewarded and exploitation is difficult, most people cooperate reliably. What does this suggest about human selfishness?

options.label: Self-interest remains the basic default; institutions merely redirect it.
Humans have both cooperative and selfish tendencies that institutions can amplify.
Cooperation can itself be a basic human tendency rather than a disguise for selfishness.
The scenario alone does not tell us much about baseline human nature.

items.text: A generation grows up under very different institutions and develops markedly different habits of trust, aggression, and cooperation. How much should this shift your view of human malleability?

options.label: Strongly; major human dispositions can be highly malleable.
Somewhat; environments matter but within substantial limits.
Little; deeper human dispositions remain mostly stable.
Not at all; the observed differences need another explanation.

items.text: Which confidence range is closest to your current belief that at least one divine or godlike reality exists?

options.label: Very unlikely.
More unlikely than likely.
Roughly balanced or deeply uncertain.
More likely than unlikely.
Very likely.

items.text: Which description is closest to your view of supernatural reality?

options.label: Nothing genuinely supernatural exists.
Supernatural reality is possible, but I am uncertain whether it exists.
At least some genuinely supernatural reality probably exists.
Supernatural beings or powers are an important part of reality.

items.text: Which description is closest to your view of what happens to a person after biological death?

options.label: The person ceases to exist.
I am substantially uncertain.
Some aspect of the person probably persists.
The person continues in a recognizably personal form.

items.text: Suppose humans disappeared and no other intelligent beings ever existed. Would reality still contain an objective purpose or goal?

options.label: Yes, objective purpose would remain.
Possibly, depending on what grounds the purpose.
No; purpose exists only through valuing or purposive agents.
None of these descriptions fits well.

items.text: Imagine a person whose life contains deep relationships, worthwhile projects, and achievements, but there is no cosmic purpose built into reality. Can that life still be genuinely meaningful?

options.label: Yes, those features can make the life objectively meaningful.
Yes, but only because people can create or confer meaning.
It can feel meaningful without there being genuine meaning beyond that experience.
No; without objective purpose, genuine meaning is absent.

items.text: A group proposes overriding one member's harmless personal project because doing so would modestly improve the group's overall welfare. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: The individual has a strong claim against being overridden.
The individual's claim matters but can be balanced against group welfare.
The group's welfare should normally take priority.
It depends on the kind of project and group relationship.

items.text: A longstanding association adopts a goal that no single member personally chose, but members jointly maintain the practices that sustain it. Can the association itself meaningfully be said to have a goal?

options.label: Yes, group-level goals can be genuine.
Yes in a useful sense, but only because of the members' coordinated activity.
No; this is only shorthand for individual members' goals.
None of these descriptions fits well.

items.text: A person loses nearly all of their former social roles and relationships but retains the same memories and personality. How much has their identity changed?

options.label: Greatly; relationships and roles are partly constitutive of who the person is.
Somewhat; they matter but do not define the core identity.
Little; identity is mainly determined by features inside the individual.
It depends on which relationships or roles were lost.

items.text: A minority group follows a way of life that most people strongly dislike but that does not violate anyone else's rights. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: The society should protect their freedom to live that way.
The society should tolerate it but need not accommodate it.
The majority may legitimately pressure them to conform.
The society may legitimately restrict the way of life because it conflicts with shared values.

items.text: You can prevent a serious harm either to one person in your own community or to one equally situated person abroad. Which should normally receive greater moral weight?

options.label: A: The person in my own community.
B: Neither; equal claims should carry equal weight.

items.text: A development project would substantially improve human living standards but permanently destroy a unique ecosystem. Which consideration should normally receive more weight?

options.label: A: The human benefits.
B: Preserving the ecosystem.

items.text: A well-run state protects rights and provides valuable services, but a peaceful resident never consented to its authority. Does the state have a moral right to coerce that resident under ordinary laws?

options.label: Yes, legitimate authority can exist without that person's consent.
Possibly, but only under demanding conditions of justification.
No, valuable performance alone does not create a right to coerce.
It depends on additional facts about consent, alternatives, or institutional procedure.

items.text: A valid law is mildly unjust. A citizen can disobey it without harming anyone. Does its legal status itself give the citizen a moral reason to obey?

options.label: Yes, a strong reason.
Yes, some independent reason.
No; only the underlying merits or consequences matter.
Only under certain kinds of political institutions.

items.text: Two governments protect rights equally well. In one, citizens meaningfully authorize rulers and laws; in the other, competent officials rule without public participation. Which has the stronger claim to legitimacy?

options.label: A: The participatory government.
B: Neither; equal performance gives them equal legitimacy.

items.text: A national rule would be uniform and simple, while locally chosen rules would vary but better reflect local conditions. Which approach should normally receive more weight?

options.label: A: Uniform centralized rules.
B: Decentralized local variation.

items.text: A regulation prevents a competent adult from making a harmless personal choice solely because officials believe the choice is bad for that person. How much freedom is lost?

options.label: A major loss of freedom because the choice was interfered with.
Some loss of freedom, even if the intervention improves welfare.
Little loss if the person's real opportunities or welfare improve.
No relevant loss of freedom if the intervention is beneficial.

items.text: A policy would greatly improve total welfare but requires knowingly violating one person's basic right. Which consideration should normally receive greater weight?

options.label: A: Respecting the person's right.
B: Producing the greater total welfare.

items.text: A community has one scarce treatment and several eligible patients. Which principle should receive the greatest weight in allocating it?

options.label: Give everyone an equal chance.
Prioritize the person in greatest medical need.
Prioritize a person who contributed more or bears special responsibility.
Prioritize someone who has not yet reached an adequate minimum of health.
Prioritize the person who would otherwise be worst off.
Honor an existing legitimate claim to the treatment.

items.text: A person legitimately owns unused land. A community could gain a large benefit by using part of it, offering full compensation, but the owner refuses. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: The owner's claim should normally control even with compensation.
The owner's claim is strong but can be overridden for sufficiently important purposes.
The community may use it when the public benefit is large and compensation is fair.
It depends on how the property was acquired and what the community needs it for.

items.text: A good can be supplied either through competitive voluntary exchange or through an equally competent allocation board. Which mechanism should normally carry more weight?

options.label: A: Competitive voluntary exchange and prices.
B: Deliberate allocation by the board.

items.text: Two people are in morally identical circumstances except for their social identity. Should the same basic moral requirement apply to both?

options.label: Yes, the same requirement should apply.
Usually, though identity can sometimes matter morally.
No, moral requirements may differ even when the other morally relevant facts are the same.
It depends on what grounds the moral requirement.

items.text: A rule normally forbids an action, but an unusual feature of one case changes what would be morally appropriate. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: The unusual feature can genuinely change the correct moral judgment.
Only very exceptional circumstances can do so.
The same rule should still determine the judgment.
It depends on what kind of rule and feature are involved.

items.text: Which description is closest to your view of moral principles?

options.label: General principles usually determine what is right once the facts are known.
General principles matter, but judgment about particulars is also indispensable.
Particular features of cases are more fundamental than general rules.
None of these descriptions fits well.

items.text: Suppose a person has no desire or goal that favors keeping a promise they freely made. Does the promise itself still give them a moral reason to keep it?

options.label: Yes, the promise itself gives a reason.
Yes, but only under certain background conditions.
No, a moral reason must connect to the person's goals or values.
None of these descriptions fits well.

items.text: A rule benefits nearly everyone but places a serious avoidable burden on one person who could reasonably object to bearing it. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: The person's reasonable rejection is a strong reason against the rule.
It matters, but may be outweighed by the benefit to others.
The overall benefit can justify the rule regardless of the person's objection.
It depends on the kind of burden and benefit.

items.text: Several people with conflicting interests must choose a common rule. Which feature gives the rule the strongest moral basis?

options.label: Each person has reason to accept it because it leaves them better off than the available alternatives.
It treats everyone's interests impartially.
It respects independent moral rights or constraints.
It encourages good character and social practices.

items.text: You can provide the same lifesaving benefit either to your sibling or to an equally needy stranger. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: The relationship gives a strong additional reason to help the sibling.
The relationship gives some additional reason.
The two claims should normally receive equal moral weight.
It depends on prior commitments or expectations within the relationship.

items.text: A person could give up an important lifelong project and thereby produce somewhat more good for others. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: They may reasonably keep the project for themselves.
It depends on how much more good the sacrifice would produce.
They should normally sacrifice the project if doing so produces more good.
Any genuine net moral gain for others defeats the self-regarding project.

items.text: A person can prevent many deaths only by permanently giving up nearly every major personal project and most discretionary income. Is that sacrifice morally required?

options.label: Yes, if the benefit to others is sufficiently large.
Some major sacrifice is required, but morality may leave room for a personal life.
Such a sacrifice may be admirable but is not morally required.
No, morality should not demand that level of self-sacrifice.

items.text: One person actively pushes someone into danger; another could easily prevent the same danger but deliberately stands aside. The resulting harm is identical. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: Actively causing the harm is morally worse.
It is usually worse, though not always.
The two can be roughly equally wrong.
It depends on further facts about duty, intention, or relationship.

items.text: Having recognized authority over important decisions affecting others.
Controlling enough resources to shape major outcomes.
Maintaining a respected public image.
Living in a stable society protected from large-scale disorder.
Respecting laws and formal rules that apply to me.
Avoiding conduct that makes social life unnecessarily difficult for people around me.
Remembering that my achievements do not make me more important than other people.
Keeping promises and commitments to people who rely on me.
Preventing irreversible damage to natural habitats.
Trying to understand people whose customs or beliefs I strongly disagree with.
A field contains many well-supported findings, but new discoveries regularly change how those findings fit together. Which is closest to your view of knowledge in such a field?

options.label: Knowledge is a changing network of interconnected claims.
Most knowledge is stable, with only peripheral details changing.
Knowledge is mainly a collection of separate facts.
It depends heavily on the field.

items.text: Which description is closest to your view of human inquiry?

options.label: For many important questions, objectively correct answers are attainable.
We can often approach truth without ever being certain we have reached it.
Important domains may have objective truths that humans cannot reliably know.
In many important domains, what counts as an answer is mainly practical or conventional.

items.text: A practice has been trusted across many generations but lacks a clear modern evidential explanation. How much epistemic weight should its longevity carry by itself?

options.label: Substantial weight; persistence can embody accumulated knowledge.
Some weight, but it needs further support.
Little weight by itself.
No additional weight solely because it is traditional.

items.text: You have a very strong intuitive impression about a claim but no independent evidence or argument for it. How much justification does the intuition provide?

options.label: Substantial prima facie justification.
Some justification, but weak without support.
Very little justification.
No genuine justification by itself.

items.text: A person sincerely believes they received a clear revelation from a divine source, but the experience cannot be independently verified. How much factual justification does the experience provide?

options.label: Substantial justification for the person.
Some justification, though independent support is still needed.
Little factual justification.
No factual justification by itself.

items.text: A mature scientific theory predicts novel results extremely well while referring to entities nobody can directly observe. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: Its success is strong evidence that at least some of those entities are approximately real.
Its success supports realism cautiously but does not settle the issue.
Its success shows only that the theory is a good predictive instrument.
None of these descriptions fits well.

items.text: Which description is closest to your view of numbers and properties such as redness or triangularity?

options.label: At least some exist independently of particular objects and human language.
They exist only insofar as they are instantiated in concrete things.
They are useful concepts or linguistic constructions rather than independent entities.
None of these descriptions fits well.

items.text: A person relies on a digital device for information that is continuously available, automatically consulted, and functionally integrated into daily reasoning. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: The device can count as part of the person's cognitive system.
It is a borderline extension of cognition.
It remains an external tool, not part of the mind.
It depends on how tightly and reliably it is integrated.

items.text: A person's aggression, trust, and risk-taking each change under different biological, social, and situational influences. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: Human behavior is usually multiply caused and difficult to reduce to one explanatory dimension.
Several causes matter, though one or two often dominate.
A small number of general causes can explain most important behavior.
It depends heavily on the behavior.

items.text: Identical twins raised apart show notable similarities in temperament despite very different environments. How much should this count as evidence for biological influence?

options.label: Strong evidence of biological contribution.
Some evidence, but not decisive.
Little evidence without ruling out other explanations.
No meaningful evidence for biological influence.

items.text: Two groups with similar biological backgrounds grow up under very different institutions and develop sharply different norms and behavior. How much should this count as evidence for environmental influence?

options.label: Strong evidence that social environment can substantially shape behavior.
Some evidence, though other causes may also matter.
Little evidence without stronger causal controls.
No meaningful evidence for environmental influence.

items.text: A person carefully weighs reasons, changes their mind, and then acts differently because of the new conclusion. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: The conscious reasoning itself can be a genuine cause of the action.
It may contribute causally alongside deeper processes.
The conscious reasoning mainly reflects causes already determining the behavior.
It depends on the mechanism linking reasoning to action.

items.text: A person repeatedly avoids a situation without knowing why, and later discovers a strong unconscious association that predicted the avoidance. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: The unconscious association can be a genuine cause of the behavior.
It may be causal, but more evidence is needed.
Calling it unconscious does not add a real causal explanation.
Only consciously represented motives should count as causes of action.

items.text: Suppose some divine reality exists. Which description is closest to your view of its nature?

options.label: It is personal or agent-like, with intentions or purposes.
It has some mind-like or purposive aspects but is not simply a person.
It is fundamentally impersonal.
Its personal or impersonal character cannot be known.

items.text: Someone prays for a specific outcome and an extremely unlikely event then occurs in exactly that way. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: Divine or supernatural intervention is a live explanatory possibility.
Intervention is possible, but the event alone provides weak evidence.
The event should be explained entirely through natural causes or chance.
It depends on additional evidence about the event.

items.text: A medically documented recovery occurs that current science cannot explain. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: A genuine miracle is a live explanatory possibility.
An unknown natural explanation is more likely, though miracle is possible.
There must be a natural explanation even if current science has not identified it.
The case alone cannot distinguish miracle from unknown natural causes.

items.text: A person believes a text is genuine divine revelation, but one teaching conflicts with their strongest independent moral judgment. Which should normally receive greater authority?

options.label: A: The believed revelation.
B: The independently reached moral judgment.

items.text: A community can gain a large practical benefit only by destroying an object it regards as sacred, with no direct harm to persons. How much moral weight should the sacred status carry?

options.label: Very high weight; sacred status can strongly constrain ordinary cost-benefit reasoning.
Some weight, but it can be outweighed by sufficient benefit.
Only the human reactions and relationships surrounding it matter.
Sacred status itself has no independent moral weight.

items.text: Religious or spiritual beliefs shaping major life decisions.
A person deliberately creates a life project that they deeply value, but the universe contains no objective purpose. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: The project can create genuine meaning.
It creates personal meaning but not objective meaning.
It can create a feeling of meaning but not genuine meaning.
Without objective purpose, such projects cannot generate real meaning.

items.text: Suppose there is no objective purpose built into human existence. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: Human life therefore lacks objective or inherent meaning.
Objective meaning could still arise from non-cosmic features of life.
Meaning can be created by persons even without objective purpose.
None of these descriptions fits well.

items.text: Two social groups are equally capable, but one is routinely placed in subordinate positions. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: The hierarchy lacks justification merely from group membership.
It could be justified only by further group-relevant reasons.
Stable group hierarchy can be acceptable even without individual-level differences.
It depends on how the hierarchy arose and functions.

items.text: A society could reduce a large status gap between groups at modest cost without changing anyone's basic rights. How important is reducing that gap?

options.label: Important in itself because group-status inequality matters.
Somewhat important, depending on how the gap arose.
Not important merely because the groups have different status.
Reducing such differences is generally undesirable.

items.text: Several people can solve a shared problem either by coordinating voluntarily or by competing for individual advantage. Which should normally be tried first?

options.label: A: Voluntary cooperation.
B: Competition among individual strategies.

items.text: Two firms can either cooperate to standardize a useful technology or compete with incompatible designs. Which process is more likely to produce better discovery and improvement?

options.label: A: Competition between designs.
B: Deliberate cooperation and standardization.

items.text: A social category has fuzzy boundaries, changes historically, and contains wide internal variation. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: The category can still reflect a deep underlying essence.
It may track some stable natural tendencies without a strict essence.
Its meaning is largely created through social classification and practice.
It is mainly a convenient label without deep underlying unity.

items.text: A category becomes socially important only after institutions begin recording it and people start organizing around it. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: Those practices can partly constitute the social category itself.
The practices amplify a category that already existed independently.
The institutions mainly discovered an independently existing social reality.
It depends on the kind of category.

items.text: A peaceful adult explicitly refuses political membership but continues living in a territory where leaving is costly. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: Without meaningful consent, coercive authority over that person is seriously weakened or absent.
Some forms of implicit consent may still justify authority.
Authority can be legitimate on grounds independent of the person's consent.
It depends on the available alternatives and institutional conditions.

items.text: An official has legal power to interfere with your choices at will but has so far always acted benevolently. How free are you from that official?

options.label: Substantially unfree because the uncontrolled power itself is dominating.
Somewhat unfree, though actual interference also matters.
Largely free so long as the official does not interfere.
It depends on safeguards, accountability, and the scope of the power.

items.text: A person faces no legal interference but lacks any realistic access to transportation, education, or basic communication needed to pursue ordinary life plans. How much political freedom do they have?

options.label: Low freedom because effective capabilities matter.
Some formal freedom, but important effective freedom is missing.
High freedom if nobody is interfering with their choices.
It depends on why those opportunities are unavailable.

items.text: A productive resource can be managed either as privately owned property or as a commons governed by its users. Which form is more legitimate in principle?

options.label: A: Private ownership with exclusion and transfer rights.
B: Common ownership governed by the users.

items.text: A workplace can be coordinated either by owner-appointed managers or by binding votes of the people working there. Which mechanism should normally carry more weight?

options.label: A: Collective or democratic decision-making by participants.
B: Managerial decision-making under ownership or contract.

items.text: A highly technical public decision has large consequences. Experts overwhelmingly agree on one policy, while most citizens prefer another. Which should normally carry more decision-making weight?

options.label: A: The expert judgment.
B: The citizens' collective preference.

items.text: A decision procedure gives every affected person equal standing and follows announced rules, but the outcome is highly unequal. How much justice does the fairness of the procedure add?

options.label: Substantial justice; fair procedure has independent value.
Some justice, though outcomes also matter.
Little justice if the substantive result is bad.
None; only the substantive outcome determines justice.

items.text: A perfectly transparent and impartial procedure predictably leaves some people without enough for basic needs. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: The outcome is unjust and gives reason to correct the result.
The outcome is troubling, though the fair procedure matters strongly.
The result should stand if the procedure was genuinely fair.
It depends on what the procedure was designed to allocate.

items.text: A wrongdoer poses no future danger, cannot be deterred, and has fully repaired the harm. Is punishment still justified simply because the wrongdoing deserves it?

options.label: Yes, deserved punishment remains justified.
Possibly, but the justification is weaker.
No, punishment needs some further beneficial purpose.
It depends on the seriousness and nature of the wrongdoing.

items.text: A punishment would strongly deter future offenses but would impose more suffering than the offender deserves. Is deterrence enough to justify it?

options.label: Yes, if the deterrent benefit is large enough.
Sometimes, but only within limits.
No, deterrence alone cannot justify disproportionate punishment.
It depends on the kind of offense and punishment.

items.text: After wrongdoing, an offender has a realistic path to rehabilitation and the victim prefers repair over punishment. Which goal should normally receive the most weight?

options.label: Repairing harm and restoring workable relationships.
Changing the offender so future wrongdoing is less likely.
Imposing deserved punishment regardless of those future benefits.
Using the response mainly to deter others.

items.text: A government can prevent the same severe harm either to one citizen or to one equally situated foreigner at the same cost. Which should normally receive greater political weight?

options.label: A: The citizen.
B: Neither; equal harms should receive equal political weight.

items.text: Two people face equal hardship, but one is a compatriot and the other is not. Does shared national membership itself create a special political obligation?

options.label: Yes, a strong special obligation.
Yes, some additional obligation.
No, equal hardship should receive equal consideration.
Only if national membership reflects further relationships or commitments.

items.text: Several overlapping institutions offer different rules for the same activity, and people can choose among them without coercive conflict. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: The institutional competition and overlap can be valuable.
It can work, but only under strong coordination rules.
One institution should ultimately have final authority.
It depends on the policy area.

items.text: A law is proposed solely because a religious authority declares the conduct sinful, with no independent public reason offered. Is that religious authority itself a legitimate basis for coercive law?

options.label: Yes, religious authority can itself ground public law.
Sometimes, if the religious authority is widely recognized by the political community.
No, coercive law requires an independent public justification.
It depends on the constitutional or institutional framework.
